title: Wehrlein wins from pole as Wittmann takes the title
dek: Pascal Wehrlein converted his first pole into a maiden DTM win for HWA Mercedes, 15.418 seconds clear of Vietoris, as Marco Wittmann's sixth place was enough to clinch the 2014 title with two races left.

chapters.title: Wittmann needs fourth place
text: The Lausitzring, the eighth round of ten, was billed as the place where the 2014 championship could be settled. A month earlier Marco Wittmann had won at the Nürburgring from pole for BMW Team RMG, and he arrived with 120 points, 64 clear of Mattias Ekström and Edoardo Mortara, who were level on 56, with Mike Rockenfeller a further three adrift on 53. Only 75 points were left on the table across the final three races.

The arithmetic was simple. If Ekström or Mortara won at the Lausitzring, Wittmann would still be champion with two races to spare provided he finished fourth or better. Wittmann admitted he could no longer avoid the subject, but his rivals had no intention of making it easy. Ekström had had a miserable Nürburgring, knocked out in an opening-lap incident, and had spoken of a weekend to forget.

Behind the Audi trio, Bruno Spengler of BMW and Christian Vietoris of Mercedes were still in the hunt for second place in the standings. Ekström said he would only congratulate Wittmann once everything was settled.

chapters.title: Wehrlein takes a maiden pole in the drizzle
text: Qualifying came after only a 15-minute free practice, because thick fog had delayed the start of track activity, so teams had almost no time to work on set-ups. Several drivers called the session a lottery. It began in damp conditions with light drizzle, and most drivers went out on slicks, but after just a few minutes Joey Hand slid into the infield gravel trap and brought out the red flag. His car had to be recovered with mechanical help, which ruled him out of the rest of the session, and race control ended Q1 on the spot, sending every car through to a lengthened Q2.

Times kept improving as the rain eased, and the top eight in Q2 went through to the last shoot-out. There Pascal Wehrlein set 1:17.547 for HWA Mercedes to take the first pole position of his DTM career and become the youngest pole-sitter in the series. Ekström was 0.057 seconds slower in the Abt Audi and Jamie Green took third for Rosberg with a lap at the very end of the session, ahead of Timo Scheider's Phoenix Audi and Daniel Juncadella's Mücke Mercedes.

Wittmann was the only BMW in the final segment and lined up seventh, 0.596 seconds off pole, and said the conditions had made it a lottery. Rockenfeller was tenth, Robert Wickens 12th and Mortara a disappointing 13th, which left him needing a miracle. Spengler struggled for balance, di Resta lined up 21st, Hand 22nd after his spin and Tomczyk, who had missed practice with a technical problem, 23rd.

chapters.title: Wehrlein escapes, Vietoris climbs
text: Rain had fallen on and off all morning, so everybody lined up on wet tyres except Mortara, who took a gamble from 13th on the grid and started on options. Wehrlein turned pole into the lead at the start, with Juncadella and Green behind him, while Ekström lost ground badly from second and was sixth early on. Mortara, meanwhile, fell towards the back on his slicks and was never a factor.

The man of the opening laps was Vietoris, who made his way from 11th on the grid to second place within the first couple of laps and then settled in behind the leader as the Mercedes drivers enjoyed the wet conditions. Wehrlein stretched his lead to roughly eleven seconds over Vietoris. Spengler was given a drive-through penalty early on for pushing another car, which ended his hopes of a recovery from 16th on the grid, and Tomczyk and Spengler had collided as well.

chapters.title: Yellow-flag drive-throughs and a loose wheel
text: The middle of the race was messy. Wehrlein had a moment on lap 16, running onto the infield grass before he got the car back under control, and lost only a couple of seconds. Juncadella then took a drive-through penalty for failing to respect yellow flags while running in the top three, which dropped him to fourth behind Scheider. Green spun twice, went through the gravel and was given a drive-through for pushing Tomczyk, while Timo Glock, Nico Müller and António Félix da Costa were all out by lap 19, 14 and six respectively.

The pit stops, with most of the field switching to option tyres from around lap 26, claimed Ekström. His Abt crew released him with the left-front wheel not properly tightened, and the wheel came off a few corners later, ending his title hopes and a race that had started on the front row. Di Resta, meanwhile, had made up places from 21st on the grid to sixth before the steering was damaged, and he was out on lap 38.

chapters.title: Scheider closes on Vietoris
text: With the track drying, the story became Scheider's charge. The Phoenix driver had been in the leading group from the start, took third after Juncadella's penalty and made up ground steadily after switching to slicks, setting the fastest lap of the race on lap 42 with a 1:19.782. Meanwhile Wittmann, sitting sixth, simply stayed out of trouble, with all the title rivals behind him.

Further back, Farfus recovered from 20th on the grid to seventh and Tomczyk from 23rd to eighth, with Molina ninth and Rockenfeller 10th after a turbulent race that left his car damaged. Mortara was classified 16th, two laps down, and Green 17th after his adventures.

chapters.title: Wehrlein wins by 15.418 seconds
text: Wehrlein took the flag after 52 laps in 1:15:47.314, 15.418 seconds ahead of his team-mate Vietoris, for his first DTM win, which made him the youngest race winner in the series' history. Scheider was only 0.263 seconds behind Vietoris at the flag after a late attack and said two more laps would have given him a realistic attack on second place. He settled for third and his first podium of the season.

Juncadella finished fourth, 18.024 seconds behind the winner, and Wickens, who had started 12th, was fifth, so Mercedes took four of the top five places. Wittmann crossed the line sixth, 48.435 seconds behind, and with the eight points that gave him the title was confirmed as champion.

chapters.title: Champion with two races to spare
text: Sixth place gave Wittmann 128 points, a 69-point lead over Vietoris, who had moved from sixth to second in the standings with 59. Ekström and Mortara both stood on 56 and Rockenfeller on 54, so nobody could catch the BMW driver with two rounds remaining. Wittmann said the key had been staying out of all the battles in a difficult race. Marquardt called it a deserved reward for a consistent year, but reminded his team that two titles were still at stake.

Wehrlein was the hero for Mercedes, celebrating his first pole and then his first win in the space of two days, and said the strategy of waiting for the track to dry before switching to options had been right. Vietoris called it a brilliant result and said he was second in the championship, which nobody would have predicted at the start of the season. Juncadella was disappointed, because he felt the penalty had cost him second place and probably his first podium. Mercedes motorsport head Wolfgang Schattling admitted the team had not expected four cars in the top five, though he stressed that its pace in the dry was still not good enough.

For Audi it was another day of good qualifying that did not become a result. Ekström said a poor start, a trip off the track and then a front-left wheel nut that was not properly tightened at his pit stop had finished his race. Scheider's podium, his first of the season, was the only bright spot, as Molina and Rockenfeller scored in ninth and 10th. Dieter Gass said the team had to analyse why its pace on the wet tyres at the start had been inconsistent, and Audi motorsport chief Wolfgang Ullrich said he was disappointed to have failed to convert good qualifying into a win again. The race was watched by 58,000 fans over the weekend.
The championship moved on to Zandvoort at the end of September, with Vietoris and three Audi drivers separated by five points in the fight for second place.

facts.v: Wehrlein won from his first DTM pole, 15.418 seconds ahead of Vietoris, and became the youngest race winner in DTM history.
